title: Goodhart's law, vanity metrics and honest KPIs
objectives: State Goodhart's law and distinguish a measure from a target
Identify vanity metrics that move without proving customer or delivery value
Design a small metric set with a counter-metric or gaming check for each
Write a one-page metric contract: definition, owner, window, and what behaviour we do not want
Defend a metric change to a team that has learned to game the old one

sources.title: Goodhart's law — Wikipedia
sources.reviewDepth: Full article retrieved 2026-10-18; classic formulation and related adages checked against the article.

verificationNotes: Wikipedia article retrieved in full on 2026-10-18. The classic formulation ('When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure'), Goodhart's 1975 monetary-policy origin, Campbell's law as a related idea, and examples (testing targets, education, citation metrics) are from the article. This lesson re-states them in Academy voice for engineering delivery; it does not claim Cretek invented the adage.
The article's point that related ideas predate Goodhart (including Campbell, Ravetz, Lucas) is noted; the common short form is used here for teaching, with the full article as source.
Vanity metrics, metric contracts, and counter-metrics are Academy extensions of the adage for CTO practice; they are not attributed to the article.
No team was measured or re-measured for this lesson. Worked examples use clearly labelled illustrative numbers.

sections.heading: The adage
sections.body:
Goodhart's law is usually quoted as: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. Charles Goodhart's 1975 observation was about monetary policy: any observed statistical regularity tends to collapse once pressure is placed on it for control purposes.

The mechanism is human. Once a number is rewarded, people optimise the number. That can mean real improvement, pure gaming, or a mix that is hard to untangle. The law does not say metrics are useless; it says the link between measure and goal breaks under reward pressure.

Related ideas in the same family: Campbell's law (quantitative social indicators used for decisions invite corruption pressures) and the general lesson from citation-index gaming that metrics of evaluation get abused.

sections.heading: Measure, target, counter-metric
sections.body:
A measure is an observation: deploy frequency, mean lead time, error rate, support contacts per customer. A target is a management commitment on that measure. The law fires when the measure becomes the target without a second check.

A counter-metric is a measure you refuse to sacrifice while chasing the primary. Examples: deploy frequency (primary) with change-failure rate and post-deploy incidents as counter-metrics; story points completed (primary, weak) with escaped defects and customer outcome metrics as counters; support contacts closed (primary) with reopen rate and CSAT as counters.

Design rule: no metric enters a review or bonus without at least one counter-metric and a written definition (numerator, denominator, window, data source). If you cannot name the gaming path, you have not finished the design.

sections.heading: Vanity metrics
sections.body:
A vanity metric looks good in a slide and does not change a decision. Typical shapes:

Cumulative totals without a rate or a denominator: '10 million events processed' with no time window, no error share, and no comparison to load.

Activity dressed as outcome: meetings held, tickets closed, PRs merged, hours logged. Each can rise while product quality and customer value fall.

Unsegmented averages that hide the tail: average latency with no p95/p99; average delivery date with no variance.

Metrics with no owner and no action: if no one would change behaviour on a red result, the metric is decoration.

Ask of every chart: what decision changes if this number moves one standard deviation? If the answer is 'none', drop it from the executive pack.

sections.heading: Say-do ratio and completion theatre
sections.body:
A common delivery vanity trap is celebrating commitments rather than outcomes. The say-do ratio is a simple honesty check: of the items you said you would do in a period, how many did you actually finish to an agreed definition of done?

Say-do below 100% is not always failure; re-planning is sometimes correct. The pathology is a permanent gap that is never explained, or a ratio gamed by shrinking the 'said' list after the fact. Freeze the commitment list at the start of the period, publish the ratio, and require a written reason for each miss. Pair it with a customer-facing outcome metric so the team cannot max the ratio by only doing trivial work.

sections.heading: A metric contract
sections.body:
Before a metric is used in governance, write a one-page contract:

Definition: exact numerator, denominator, filters, and exclusions.
Window: hour, day, sprint, month; state it on every chart.
Source system and owner: which system of record, who fixes a data bug.
Intended decision: what a red or green result is allowed to change.
Counter-metrics: what must not get worse while this improves.
Anti-gaming note: the most likely way this number will be gamed, and how you will detect it.
Review cadence: when the contract itself is re-read.

If the contract cannot be written in a page, the metric is not ready for a board slide.

workedExample.title: Two teams, two metric failures (illustrative)
workedExample.body:
Team A: leadership sets a target of 40 PRs merged per engineer per month. Merged PRs climb. Review depth collapses, small cosmetic changes split across PRs, and production incidents rise. The measure became the target; the counter-metrics (incident rate, review quality sample) were absent. Fix: replace the volume target with a flow metric (lead time for changes) plus change-failure rate and a monthly review-quality sample; drop the PR count from the exec pack.

Team B: 'support contacts resolved per day' is targeted. Agents close tickets before the customer confirms. Reopen rate doubles; CSAT falls. Fix: count resolved only after 48 hours without reopen; add reopen rate and CSAT as equal-weight counters.

Numbers above are SIMULATED teaching cases, not Cretek telemetry. The point is the pattern: every target needs a written definition, a window, an owner, and a counter-metric.

misconceptions: Believing removing all targets fixes Goodhart. Direction and constraints still matter; unmeasured work drifts.
Using a metric in a bonus before its anti-gaming note exists.
Reading a cumulative total as health.
Averaging away the p99 and the unhappy customers.
Changing the metric definition mid-period to improve the story.
Treating DORA or flow metrics as targets to max rather than signals to interpret with counters.
learn.explainTask: In 120 words or fewer, explain to a delivery manager why you will not put 'PRs merged per person' on the team scorecard, and what you will put instead.

knowledgeCheck.question: Goodhart's law in its common form is:
options: When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure
Only audited metrics matter
If you cannot measure it, it does not exist
Faster is always better
knowledgeCheck.why: The classic short form: reward pressure breaks the measure's link to the goal.

knowledgeCheck.question: A counter-metric exists to:
options: Replace the primary metric in the board pack
Detect when the primary is being gamed or is harming something else that matters
Double the reporting effort
Make averages look better
knowledgeCheck.why: Counters catch gaming and side effects while chasing the primary.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which is most likely a vanity metric for an executive update?
options: Change failure rate with a 30-day window and owner
Cumulative 'events processed' with no rate, error share, or decision attached
p95 latency trend with an alert threshold
Say-do ratio with a frozen commitment list
knowledgeCheck.why: An unsegmented cumulative total that changes no decision is decoration.

knowledgeCheck.question: Say-do ratio measures:
options: How fast the team types
Of the items committed in a period, how many were finished to the agreed definition of done
Lines of documentation written
Number of meetings declined
knowledgeCheck.why: It is a completion honesty check against a frozen commitment list, not an activity count.

knowledgeCheck.question: What must exist before a metric is used in bonuses or public scoreboards?
options: A slide template
A written contract: definition, window, owner, decision, counter-metrics, anti-gaming note
A vendor dashboard
Unanimous team love for the number
knowledgeCheck.why: Without the contract, you are inviting the exact failure the law describes.

knowledgeCheck.question: Team raises 'tickets closed per day'. Agents close without customer confirmation and reopens spike. Best first fix:
options: Raise the daily target further
Define resolved only after a confirmation window; track reopen rate and CSAT as counters
Hide the reopen data
Stop measuring support
knowledgeCheck.why: Tighten the definition and add counters; do not hide the damage or double down on the gamed target.

build.business: Cretek needs delivery and reliability numbers a board can trust without teaching the organisation to game them. This is the measurement discipline in the CTO Operating System.
build.problem: Audit one real metric pack (or a labelled SIMULATED pack), rewrite it as metric contracts with counter-metrics, and demonstrate a gaming scenario in a small local simulator.
requirements: List every metric currently shown to leadership (or simulate a realistic pack) and tag each: decision-driving, diagnostic, or vanity
For each metric you keep, write a one-page contract: definition, window, source, owner, intended decision, counter-metrics, anti-gaming note
For each vanity metric, write what it was replaced with and why the old one is dropped
Build a local simulation or analysis script: a gamed scenario (for example PR-splitting under a volume target) showing the primary rising while a counter-metric falls
Tests or assertions that flag metrics missing a contract field or missing a counter-metric
A one-page say-do or outcome summary suitable for a product owner
Label every figure REAL, ASSUMPTION or SIMULATED
constraints: Do not put individual performance ranking on a gamed volume metric
Do not change definitions mid-period without a written note in the contract
Must run locally with a single command for the audit tool and its tests
build.design: One page: metric inventory, keep/drop rules, and the simulation scenario.
acceptance: No metric remains without definition, window, owner and decision
Each keeper has at least one counter-metric
Simulation shows primary up / counter down under gaming
Vanity drops are justified, not silent
build.deliverable: Metric inventory, contracts, audit script with tests, and one-page summary in a repository referenced by link or path.

defend.scenario: A delivery manager loves a new 'merged PRs' dashboard from a vendor. You must argue for a smaller, honest metric set without sounding anti-transparency.
prompts: What decision changes when merged-PR count moves?
How will this be gamed within one sprint?
What counter-metric would you attach before this goes to the board?
What will you still show from the vendor pack, and with what window?
How do you handle the team's fear that fewer vanity charts means less credit for hard work?

rubric.criterion: Names the gaming path and a detection method
Proposes a smaller contract-backed metric set, not no metrics
Clear language for a non-analyst delivery manager
